newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Stranded tourists airlifted from Australian floods.
newsitem.headline: Stranded tourists airlifted from Australian floods.

text.p: Nine European tourists, stranded by floods for four days at a road workers' camp in the Australian outback, were airlifted to safety on Monday.
Police said the tourists, believed to be German, Austrian and Dutch, were stranded on the Oodnadatta track in the north of South Australia state. They were believed to be in good health.
The publican of the nearby William's Creek Hotel, Peter Moore, said the tourists were caught last week by rising waters and forced to walk to the camp, where food supplies were dwindling.

"Small gullies we did not even know were rivers are now 1.5 km (a mile) of raging torrents of water," Moore told Reuters by telephone. William's Creek, home to just two families, has also been isolated by flood waters, stranding overseas tourists.

"We are surrounded by a lot of water in the middle of the desert," said Italian tourist Martina Primoth, who had been stranded for nearly a week at the William's Creek Hotel, about 900 km (550 miles) north of Adelaide.
"It is quite special and it is a bit of an adventure," Primoth said, adding she and a fellow traveller were painting the hotel's interior while they waited for roads to reopen.
Police spokesman Bob Howe said a rescue plane was due late on Monday to fly over the Oodnadatta track to ensure no other travellers were stranded.

Rainfall of up to 14 inches (35 cms), more than a four-year average total for some areas, has fallen in the past four days in South Australia, causing flooding of up to 250,000 sq km (96,520 sq miles) of desert and pastoral land and isolating homesteads and Aboriginal communities.
Flooding has cut off the transcontinental rail service, which runs between Adelaide and Sydney, at Broken Hill.
Vast tracts of Western Australia's Pilbara region are under flood, with the coastal town of Onslow expected to be isolated for four days as floodwaters surge towards the Indian Ocean.
